stories.title: The Dark Cave
stories.text:
# The Dark Cave

The small white rabbit was gone.

The shy young boy stood at the mouth of the cave and called its name softly. His voice was thin in the quiet afternoon. Only the wind in the pine trees answered him.

Every day before this, the boy and the rabbit had walked together on the gentle path near his village. The boy did not have many friends. He liked animals more than people. The rabbit was small and warm, and it always sat in his lap when he read his books. He loved it very much.

But today the rabbit had jumped from his arms. It ran fast up the mountain. The boy ran after it, his small feet slipping on the loose stones. He called and called. Then he saw a flash of white fur near the rocks — and the rabbit went straight into the dark cave.

The boy stopped at the entrance. His hands felt cold.

He was afraid of the dark. He had always been afraid of the dark. At home, he slept with a small lamp by his bed. His mother said he would grow out of it one day, but he had not.

The sun was low now. The mountain air smelled of wet stone and old leaves. Somewhere inside the cave, he heard a soft sound. A small thump. Then nothing.

"Please come out," he whispered.

The rabbit did not come out.

The boy looked back down the path. The village was far away. His mother would be cooking rice now. The smoke from the kitchens would be rising into the orange sky. If he ran home, someone could come back with him. A bigger person. A braver person.

But the sun was going. And the cave was very dark. And the rabbit was very small.

He took one step forward. The cool air of the cave touched his face. He took another step. His heart was beating loud in his ears.

Inside, the light became weak. He put one hand on the cold wall. The stone felt rough under his fingers. He moved slowly, one small step at a time. Drip. Drip. Water was falling somewhere far inside.

"It is only a cave," he said to himself. His voice sounded strange in the dark. "It is only a cave."

He walked deeper. The light from the entrance grew smaller behind him. He could not see his own feet now. He stopped. He wanted to turn around. He wanted to run.

Then he heard it. A small, soft cry. The rabbit.

The boy forgot the dark. He moved toward the sound. His hand felt the wall, then empty air, then the wall again. The cry came once more, closer now. He bent down. His fingers touched something warm and soft. Fur.

The rabbit was shaking. One of its back legs was bent the wrong way. It had fallen between two stones.

The boy was crying a little, but his hands were calm. He gently lifted the rabbit out. He held it close to his chest. He could feel its tiny heart beating fast against his.

"I have you," he said. "I have you now."

He turned around. The small light at the cave entrance looked far away, but he could see it. He walked toward it, slow and careful, the rabbit warm in his arms.

When he stepped out into the orange light, the wind touched his wet face. The pine trees moved softly. Below him, the small lights of the village were beginning to shine, one by one.

He sat down on a flat stone and looked at the rabbit in his arms. It blinked up at him with one dark, tired eye.

The boy smiled, and it was a small smile, but it was new.

That night, he slept with no lamp.

stories.title: The Last Catch
stories.text:
# The Last Catch

The old fisherman stared at the line where the dark water met the darker sky, and he knew the storm was already deciding for him.

He had been at sea since before noon. The afternoon light was thin now, the kind of grey-gold that fishermen along this coast had learned to fear. To the east, the clouds had stacked themselves into a black wall, and the wind had begun to change its voice — softer one moment, then sharp and quick the next, like something testing the boat before it struck.

His nets were almost empty.

Three small fish lay in the wooden bucket at his feet. Three. After eight hours. He could not go home with three fish. Not today.

The younger men in the harbour had laughed at him that morning, the way they had been laughing for two years now. *The old man and his old boat,* they would say, not quite loud enough for him to hear, but never quiet enough either. He had not answered them. He had simply pushed off from the dock and pointed the bow toward the deep water, the way he had done for forty years, the way his father had done before him.

He knew this sea. He knew where the big fish ran when the pressure dropped before a storm. He had learned it from the man whose photograph he kept folded inside his wallet, beneath the worn leather, where no one would find it. The boy in the photograph was sixteen. The boy in the photograph had been his son.

The fisherman gripped the wheel and tried not to think about the photograph.

That had been the secret he carried for eleven years — the storm that had taken his son, and the truth that he had been the one steering the boat that night. He had chased one more catch. The wind had turned. The wave had come from the wrong side. And by the time he understood what was happening, the boy was already in the water and the rope was already gone.

He had not spoken his son's name out loud since the funeral.

The wind pushed against the side of the boat now, harder. The first heavy drops of rain hit the deck like small stones. To the west, his village was a thin grey line on the horizon, perhaps an hour back if he turned now. To the east, where the storm was, the water was deep and rich and full of the fish that fed on the change in pressure. He could feel them down there. He had always been able to feel them.

One good catch. One full net. He could pay for the new engine. He could silence the laughter. He could, for one evening at least, walk into the harbour like the man he used to be.

He turned the wheel slightly toward the storm.

The boat tilted. Cold spray hit his face. And then, in the wind, he heard it — not clearly, but the way memory sometimes speaks, in a voice you have not let yourself hear for years. *Papa. Papa, the rope.*

His hands stopped on the wheel.

For a long moment he stood there, the rain running down his cheeks, his old heart beating like a drum he could not slow. He looked out at the wall of black cloud. He looked down at the three small fish in the bucket. He looked at his hands — older than he remembered, stained with salt, shaking slightly.

He thought of the boy. Not as he had been in the water that night, but as he had been on a quiet afternoon long before, sitting beside him on the dock, swinging his feet, asking questions about the names of clouds.

The fisherman closed his eyes.

"Enough," he whispered. "Enough now."

He turned the wheel back toward the village. The wind fought him for a moment, and then, almost gently, it let him go.

The rain came harder as he steered home. He did not hurry. He let the old boat find its own pace through the rising water, the way an old man walks home in a familiar street. Somewhere behind him, the storm broke fully over the deep water — a place he would not visit again.

When he reached the harbour, the lamps along the dock were just beginning to flicker on. The young men were gone, hiding from the rain. He tied up the boat with hands that no longer shook. He carried the bucket of three small fish up the wooden steps.

At the top, he stopped, and for the first time in eleven years, he said his son's name out loud.

It sounded like the sea, finally letting something go.

stories.title: The Warm Tea
stories.text:
# The Warm Tea

The boy pulled his thin jacket closer and tried to stop shaking.

The market street was almost empty now. The sellers were packing up their boxes. The lights above the small shops were turning on, one by one, soft and yellow against the cold blue evening. A woman walked past him with a heavy bag. She did not look at him. No one looked at him.

Every day, the boy sat in the same corner, between the bread shop and the closed flower stall. He was nine years old, maybe ten. He was not sure anymore. He had been on this street for a long time. In the summer, it was easier. In the summer, the stones were warm and the people were kind and sometimes they gave him fruit.

But this was winter. And winter was different.

His hands were red. His feet had no feeling. He had not eaten since the morning, when a man had thrown him half a piece of bread, the way you throw food to a dog. He had eaten it anyway. He was not proud anymore.

The wind moved down the street. It pushed an empty plastic bag past his feet. He watched it go.

He was tired. He was so tired. He closed his eyes for a moment and tried to remember his mother's face, but the memory was getting smaller every year, like a photograph left out in the sun.

Then he felt something. Someone was sitting down next to him.

He opened his eyes.

It was an old woman. She was small and round, wrapped in a brown coat that was older than he was. She had a soft face with many lines, and white hair under a grey scarf. She did not speak. She just sat down beside him on the cold stones, slowly, the way old people sit down, and she put a small bag on her lap.

The boy waited for her to say something. Old people sometimes shouted at him. Sometimes they told him to move. Sometimes they asked questions he did not want to answer.

The old woman did not do any of these things.

She opened her bag. She took out a small metal cup, the kind you use for travel. Steam rose from it into the cold air. The boy could smell it — sweet, warm, with a little ginger. He had not smelled anything like that in a long time.

The old woman poured a small amount of the tea into the cup's lid. She held the cup in both her hands for a moment. Then, without looking at him, without saying one word, she passed the cup to the boy.

His hands moved before he could think. He took it.

It was warm. So warm. He held it against his chest first, just to feel it, and his fingers began to come back to life. Then he drank. The tea was sweet and hot and it went all the way down inside him, into a cold place he had forgotten about.

He did not cry. He had not cried in a long time. But something inside him moved.

The old woman drank from the lid. They sat together in silence. The wind blew. The lights above the shops grew brighter as the sky grew darker. Somewhere, a dog was barking. Somewhere, a mother was calling her child home.

When the cup was empty, the old woman took it back gently. She put it in her bag. Then she stood up, slowly, and she put one soft, wrinkled hand on top of the boy's head, just for a moment.

She walked away into the evening.

The boy sat there for a long time. The warmth of the tea was still inside him. The warmth of her hand was still on his head.

He was still hungry. He was still cold. Nothing had really changed.

And yet.

The next morning, when a small girl dropped her hat in the street and did not see, the boy ran after her and gave it back. She smiled at him. He smiled too — and it was the first time in a long, long time.

stories.title: The Morning Bread
stories.text:
# The Morning Bread

Every morning, before the sun came up, the young baker put one small loaf of bread on the windowsill.

The town was still sleeping. The cobblestone streets were quiet. The sky was soft and grey, and the spring air smelled of rain from the night before. Inside the bakery, the ovens were warm. The young baker had been awake since three o'clock, the way he was every day.

He rolled the dough. He shaped the bread. He pulled the hot loaves out of the oven with his strong, careful hands. But always, before the bakery opened, he chose one loaf — the smallest, the prettiest, the one with the golden top — and he placed it on the windowsill that faced the street.

He did this for one reason only.

At six o'clock, every morning, the flower seller from across the street walked past his window on her way to the market. She was a young woman with quiet eyes and brown hands. She always carried a heavy basket of flowers. And every morning, when she saw the small loaf on his windowsill, she stopped, smiled, and took it. She thought it was a gift from the bakery for early customers. She did not know it was for her.

The young baker had loved her for two years.

He had never told her. Not once. He was a quiet man, and his words always disappeared when she was near. So instead, every morning, he gave her bread. And every morning, she said "thank you" through the window, and walked on, and he watched her until she turned the corner.

This spring morning was the same as all the other mornings. He placed the loaf on the windowsill. He waited. The clock above the oven moved slowly. Six o'clock came. He looked through the glass.

She was there.

But today, she did not take the bread. Today, she stopped, looked at it for a long moment, and then she opened the door of the bakery and walked inside.

The young baker's hands went still on the counter.

"Good morning," she said softly. Her voice was different inside the shop. Closer. Real.

"Good morning," he said. His own voice sounded far away.

She put her basket of flowers on the floor. She held the small loaf in her hands. She looked at it, and then she looked at him.

"My friend works here in the afternoon," she said. "She told me. She said the morning loaf is not for the customers. She said it is only for me. She said you choose the prettiest one. Every day."

The baker could not speak. His face was warm. The smell of fresh bread was all around them.

"Is it true?" she asked.

He wanted to say no. He wanted to laugh, and say it was just a mistake, and send her away with the bread the way he always did. But she was looking at him, and her eyes were quiet and waiting, and he was so tired of being quiet.

"Yes," he said. "It is true."

She did not move. The bakery was silent except for the soft sound of the oven.

Then, slowly, she put the bread down on the counter between them. She looked at it for a moment. Then she looked up.

"For two years?" she said.

"For two years," he said.

She smiled. It was a small smile, but it was the kind that started at the eyes first.

"Tomorrow," she said softly, "I will come a little earlier. So we can eat it together."

She picked up her basket. She walked to the door. At the door, she stopped, and she looked back at him, and her face was warm and shy and full of something he had been waiting to see for a long, long time.

Then she was gone.

The young baker stood alone in his warm bakery. The small loaf sat on the counter, untouched. Outside, the spring sun was just beginning to rise over the cobblestone street.

He smiled. And for the first time in two years, the morning felt long enough.

stories.title: The First Day
stories.text:
# The First Day

The soup was on the floor.

The young waiter looked down at the broken bowl, then at the orange stain spreading across the clean wooden floor, then at the kitchen door, then at the floor again. He had been working at the restaurant for exactly one hour and seventeen minutes.

"It is fine," he whispered to himself. "It is fine. Everything is fine."

It was not fine.

The small family restaurant was on a quiet street in the middle of town. It had ten tables, soft yellow walls, and the best tomato soup in the city. The owner was a short, round man with grey hair and a loud laugh. He had hired the young waiter only yesterday. "You will be great," the owner had said, smiling. "Just do not break anything."

The young waiter had now broken three things.

He quickly cleaned the soup with a towel. He hid the broken pieces of the bowl behind a plant. He took a deep breath. He could do this. He was a professional. He was wearing a black shirt and everything.

The door of the restaurant opened.

"Oh no," said the owner from the kitchen. "Oh no, oh no, oh no."

"What?" said the young waiter.

"It is him."

"Who?"

"The food critic."

The young waiter turned around slowly. A tall man in a grey coat had walked in. He had a thin face, small glasses, and the kind of expression that said he had eaten lunch in better places than this.

"He writes for the big newspaper," the owner whispered. "If he likes the food, we will have customers for a year. If he does not like it..." The owner did not finish.

"What do I do?" the young waiter said.

"Be normal! Be calm! Be a good waiter!"

The young waiter walked toward the tall man. His shoes made a small squelching sound. He looked down. He had stepped in the soup.

"Good afternoon," he said brightly, hiding his orange shoe behind his other foot.

The tall man looked at him over his glasses. "Good afternoon. Table for one."

"Yes! One table! For one! Right this way, sir!"

The young waiter walked the man to the best table by the window. He pulled out the chair. The chair, somehow, made a loud rude sound as it scraped the floor. The tall man's eyebrows went up.

"The menu, sir," said the young waiter. He handed the man the menu. The menu was, he noticed too late, slightly damp.

The tall man held the damp menu by one corner.

"I will have the tomato soup," he said carefully, "and the chicken."

The young waiter ran to the kitchen. "Soup and chicken!" he shouted. The owner gave him a look that meant *please stop shouting*.

Five minutes later, the young waiter walked back with a tray. The bowl of soup. The plate of chicken. He moved slowly. He moved carefully. He was going to do this perfectly.

He placed the soup on the table.

He placed the chicken on the table.

He stepped back, and his foot hit the leg of the chair behind him, and the tray flew up, and the empty water glass on the tray flipped through the air in a perfect circle, and landed — somehow, miraculously — right in the middle of the soup.

A small wave of tomato soup splashed onto the tall man's grey coat.

The restaurant went silent.

The young waiter stared. The owner, in the kitchen door, put both hands over his face.

The tall man looked down at his coat. He looked at the glass standing in his soup. He looked at the young waiter. And then, slowly, he began to laugh. A real, loud, surprised laugh.

"Young man," he said, wiping his eyes, "I have eaten in two hundred restaurants this year. This is the most memorable lunch I have had."

He took out a small notebook. He began to write.

The next week, the newspaper came out. The review said the food was wonderful, the soup was the best in the city — and the service was, and these were his exact words, *unforgettable*.

The young waiter kept the newspaper in his pocket for a year.

stories.title: The Locked Drawer
stories.text:
# The Locked Drawer

The key did not match any door in the house, and that was what made the young woman keep looking.

She had been at her aunt's house for four days. The lawyer had given her the keys at the funeral, along with a thin folder of papers and a small brass key on a separate ring — old, worn smooth, attached to nothing. *Your aunt asked that you have this,* the lawyer had said. He had not known what it was for.

The house stood at the edge of the small town, where the cobblestone street ended and the fields began. It was the first week of autumn. The leaves outside the kitchen window had just started to turn, and in the mornings a thin mist gathered along the low stone wall in the garden. Inside, the rooms still smelled faintly of her aunt — of lavender, and old books, and the particular dryness of a house where the windows had not been opened in too long.

The young woman had not really known her aunt.

That was the truth she had been carrying since the funeral. Her aunt had been her mother's older sister, the strange one, the one who had never married, who had lived alone in this same house for forty years, who came to family lunches twice a year and barely spoke. The family had not been unkind about her, exactly. But they had not been warm. *She was always a little odd,* her mother used to say, in the tone people use when they have decided not to ask any more questions.

The young woman had not asked questions either. She regretted that now.

On the fourth evening, she found the drawer.

It was in the small writing desk in the upstairs bedroom — a narrow drawer beneath the main one, almost hidden, the kind of drawer you would only notice if you were looking. She had been clearing the desk to sell. When she pulled at it, it did not move. Locked.

She sat back. She felt the brass key in her pocket.

It fit.

Inside the drawer was a stack of letters. Maybe sixty of them, tied with a faded blue ribbon, the paper soft and yellowed at the edges. The handwriting on the top envelope was careful and slanted. The address was the house she was sitting in. There was no stamp. None of the letters had stamps. They had never been mailed.

She untied the ribbon with hands that had become slow.

The first letter was dated forty-one years ago.

*My dear,* it began. *They told me today that you are getting married next month. I will not write to congratulate you. I do not have the strength for that kind of lie. But I want you to know that I am happy you are happy, even if it is not with me. I will keep this letter, the way I keep all the others, because there is nowhere to send them anymore.*

The young woman read it twice. Then she read the next one.

And the next.

They were all written to the same person — a man, never named, only ever called *my dear* or *you*. They spanned forty years. Some were a single paragraph. Others ran for pages. They described small things, mostly: the garden in summer, a piece of music on the radio, a strange dream, a winter when the pipes froze. They described, also, a love that had simply continued, year after year, without any reply, without any hope, without any need for either.

Near the bottom of the stack, the young woman found a different envelope. Thicker. The handwriting was different — heavier, more masculine. This one had been mailed. The postmark was nine years old.

She opened it.

It was a single page. *I have looked for you for thirty-two years,* it began. *I am old now. My wife passed away last spring. I do not know if this letter will reach you, or if you will want it to. But I have never stopped, not for one day, and I had to write at least once before there was no more time.*

It was signed with a first name only. A short, simple name.

The young woman sat very still in the upstairs bedroom of the small house at the edge of the town. The autumn wind moved softly against the window. Somewhere in the garden, a branch tapped against the stone wall.

She thought of her aunt — the quiet woman at the family lunches, the one who had never married, the one they had all decided was simply odd. She thought of her own mother saying, *she was always a little strange.*

She thought of forty years of unsent letters in a locked drawer.

She folded the man's letter carefully. She placed it back among the others. She tied the blue ribbon again, slowly, the way her aunt must have tied it many times.

Then she went downstairs to find her phone, and to find a small, simple name, and to see if a man very old was still alive somewhere — and if he was, to tell him, gently, that the letters had been written, all of them, every year, without missing one.

stories.title: The Humming Key
stories.text:
# The Humming Key

The key was warm in her hand, and it was singing.

The young girl sat on the wet sand and looked at it. The storm had ended only an hour ago. The sea was still grey and tired. All along the beach, there were small things the waves had thrown up — pieces of wood, bits of rope, broken shells, a single shoe with no owner. She knew all of these things. She had been collecting lost things on this beach for as long as she could remember.

But she had never found anything like this.

The key was small and silver, and it was made of a metal she did not know. It was not heavy. When she held it close to her ear, it made a soft, low sound — not quite a song, but almost. A hum, like a bee that was very far away.

She put the key in her pocket. She walked home along the cobblestone street of her small seaside village. The early summer sun was coming back through the clouds. The fishing boats were rocking in the harbour. She nodded at the old man who sold bread, and he nodded back, and he did not see the key in her pocket because nobody could see it but her.

She knew that already. She did not know how she knew, but she knew.

In her small bedroom, she took out the wooden box where she kept all her lost things. There were forty-six things in it. A red button. A child's toy car with three wheels. A silver earring. A folded piece of paper with writing she could not read. She put the humming key inside the box, gently, on top of the others.

The humming stopped.

She blinked. She picked the key up again. The hum came back, soft and warm.

She put it down. The hum stopped.

She picked it up. The hum returned.

"You only sing for me," she whispered.

That night, she could not sleep. The key was on her bedside table, silent now, but somehow she could feel it watching her. She got up and went to the window. The moon was bright over the sea. The waves were quiet again. And then, very softly, she heard the hum.

The key was singing without her.

She picked it up. The hum grew stronger. She walked to the window, and the hum grew stronger still. She opened the window. The salt air came in.

She followed the hum.

It led her down the cobblestone street, past the sleeping bakery, past the closed flower shop, past the harbour where the boats were rocking softly. It led her to the very end of the village, where the cliffs began. There, at the foot of the cliffs, she saw a small wooden door in the rock. She had walked past this rock a hundred times. There had never been a door before.

The key fit perfectly.

She turned it.

The door opened, and warm yellow light came out, and inside the rock there was a small room — a small, impossible room — and the room was full.

It was full of every lost thing.

She saw a glove she had lost two winters ago. She saw her grandmother's reading glasses, the ones the family had searched for after the funeral. She saw a small blue boat she had played with when she was four. She saw letters and rings and toys and shoes and photographs, and she saw, hanging gently in the warm air, the laugh of a baby she did not know but somehow remembered.

In the middle of the room, an old woman was sitting in a wooden chair. Her face was kind. Her eyes were the colour of the sea after a storm.

"You have been finding my things for a long time," the old woman said.

"They are not yours," the girl said. "They are everyone's."

The old woman smiled. "Yes. That is why I needed someone like you."

The girl looked around the room. "What is this place?"

"A place where lost things wait," the old woman said softly. "Some things are meant to come back. Some things are not. Someone must choose."

The girl was quiet for a long moment. Then she said, "Will you teach me?"

The old woman held out her hand.

The young girl walked into the warm yellow room, and somewhere in the village above, a grandmother turned in her sleep and dreamed of her old reading glasses, and smiled.

stories.title: The Festival Weekend
stories.text:
# The Festival Weekend

The train pulled into the small station at four in the afternoon, and the young man stepped down onto a platform that had not changed in seven years.

The heat hit him first. Late summer in the inland towns was always heavier than he remembered. The air smelled of cut grass and something fried — the festival booths, probably, already setting up in the square. A single cracked bench. A vending machine that had been broken when he was sixteen and was, somehow, still broken now. A station master who nodded at him without recognition, even though they had gone to the same school.

He shouldered his bag and walked into town.

He had not planned to come back this weekend. He had not planned to come back at all, if he was honest. But his mother had called, and his mother had said the festival, and his mother had said *your old friend asks about you sometimes,* and now here he was, in a town he had spent his whole adolescence trying to leave.

He walked the familiar streets slowly. The bakery had a new sign. The bookshop was gone, replaced by a phone repair store. The big tree in the central square — the one he and his friend had carved their initials into when they were fourteen, drunk for the first time on cheap rice wine, certain that everything ahead of them would be enormous — was still there. He did not look for the initials. He was not ready.

His friend was sitting outside the small café, exactly where he had said he would be.

The young man stopped on the other side of the street and just looked, for a moment, at the person he had once known better than himself.

His friend was heavier now. Not much, but enough that he noticed. He was wearing a faded work shirt and the kind of comfortable, slightly tired expression that the young man had only ever seen on adults. He was reading something on his phone. He looked, the young man thought with a small painful surprise, like a man.

They had stopped talking three years ago. There had been no fight. There had only been a slow, gentle disappearing, the way a path becomes a field if no one walks it.

The young man crossed the street.

"You came," his friend said, looking up. He did not stand. He smiled, but it was a careful smile.

"I came."

They ordered coffee. The conversation was, at first, polite in the way conversations are polite when neither person knows where the safe ground is. They talked about the train. The heat. His friend's work at the agricultural cooperative. The young man's job in the city, which sounded, when he described it out loud here, smaller and sillier than it had ever sounded to him before.

Then there was a silence. A long one.

"I was angry at you," his friend said finally. He said it without heat, the way you describe the weather of a year ago. "For a long time. When you stopped writing back."

The young man turned his cup slowly in his hands. "I know."

"You thought you had outgrown this place." His friend smiled, and there was something tired in it, but no longer angry. "You thought you had outgrown me."

"That is not — " the young man began. Then he stopped, because his friend was right, and his friend had always been the one who could see through him.

"It is alright," his friend said quietly. "Some people are meant to leave. I never thought less of you for it. I only thought less of you for pretending you had not."

The coffee was bitter. Somewhere down the street, the festival musicians were beginning to test their instruments — a few sharp notes, then silence, then a slow tuning sound that filled the late afternoon.

They walked together to the festival as the sun began to sink. The square was filling up. Children with painted faces. Old men playing chess at a table they had probably been playing at for thirty years. The lanterns were going on, one by one, just as they always had. The young man recognized almost no one, and yet he recognized everything.

"You will leave on Sunday," his friend said, not as a question.

"Yes."

"And you will not come back for a long time."

The young man did not answer. He looked at the lanterns. He looked at his friend's profile against the warm orange light.

"Maybe," he said. "Maybe not."

His friend laughed, softly. "It is the same thing."

They stood and watched the festival for a long time. Somewhere near the central tree, a child was crying about a balloon. Somewhere else, an old song was beginning. The young man understood, with a kind of slow ache he did not entirely mind, that he was not going to move back here. He had not become this town's kind of man. The city had taken something from him that this place would not return.

But he understood, also, that his friend had not been wrong about him — and that admitting it was a kind of homecoming too. Smaller than the one his mother had hoped for. But real.

When the festival fireworks finally began, the two of them tilted their heads back at exactly the same moment, the way they had done every summer of their childhood, and for the length of the show, they were boys again.

Then the last light faded. They walked back through the warm streets in a comfortable, adult silence.

At the corner where they would part, his friend put a hand briefly on his shoulder.

"Write back this time," he said. "Even just sometimes."

The young man nodded. He meant it. He thought, with some surprise, that he might actually do it.

stories.title: The Room Above
stories.text:
# The Room Above

The footsteps started again at midnight, and this time, the boy decided to go and look.

He sat up in his bed. His new bedroom was small and cold. The wooden walls of the old house made small sounds at night, the way old houses do, but the footsteps above his head were not one of those sounds. The footsteps were soft and slow. They walked from one side of the room above to the other. Then they stopped. Then, after a few minutes, they walked back.

He had been hearing them for six nights.

His family had moved into the old wooden house at the edge of the small mountain town only a week ago. His father said the house was a good house. His mother said the house had "character." The boy was nine years old, and he thought the house was strange. The wind made the windows sing. The stairs were too steep. And the room above his bedroom was always, always locked.

"We do not need that room," his mother had said, when he asked. "It is full of old furniture. Maybe in the spring we will clean it."

But something was walking in that room every night.

The boy had not told his parents. He was not sure why. Maybe because his mother already worried too much. Maybe because his father would say it was the wind, and he would not like being told it was the wind, because he knew it was not.

Tonight, he had a plan.

He got out of bed. He put on his slippers. He took the small flashlight from under his pillow — he had hidden it there in the afternoon. He listened. The footsteps were walking again. Soft. Slow.

He opened his bedroom door very carefully. The hallway was dark. The old wooden floor was cold even through his slippers. He walked toward the narrow stairs that went up to the locked room. He did not turn on the flashlight yet. The moonlight from the hallway window was enough.

At the bottom of the stairs, he stopped.

The footsteps stopped too.

The boy's heart was loud in his ears. He waited. Nothing. He took one step up. The wooden stair made a small *creak*. He waited again. The footsteps did not come back.

He climbed the stairs, slowly, one by one. At the top, there was a small wooden door. He had been told it was locked.

He pushed it.

It opened.

The boy held his breath. He turned on the flashlight.

The room was full of old furniture, just like his mother had said — a tall cupboard, a covered chair, a wooden box with a broken lid, all wrapped in white sheets that looked grey in the small beam of light. The air was cold and smelled of dust and old paper.

There was no one there.

He stood in the doorway. He moved the flashlight slowly around the room. White sheets. Wooden floor. A small window at the far end with the moon shining through it. Nothing else.

Then he heard it. A very small sound. Not a footstep this time. A tiny, soft *meow*.

The boy turned the flashlight toward the sound.

Under the wooden box, two small green eyes looked back at him.

It was a cat.

A small grey cat, very thin, with fur the colour of dust. It blinked at him. It did not run. It only sat there, in its small hiding place under the wooden box, looking at him as if it had been waiting for him for a long time.

The boy knelt down slowly. He held out his hand. The cat sniffed his fingers. Then, very gently, the cat walked out from under the box and pushed its small head against his palm.

It was warm. So warm.

The boy understood, then. The cat had probably been living in this room for a long time — maybe before his family had even moved in. There must be a small hole somewhere in the wall, big enough for a cat. Every night, when the house went quiet, the cat came out of its hiding place and walked across the room, the way cats do.

Footsteps. Just footsteps. Just a small, lonely cat looking for company.

The boy lifted the cat carefully into his arms. It was almost weightless. It pushed its face into his neck and began to purr — a deep, surprising sound from such a small body.

"Come on," the boy whispered. "My room is warmer."

He carried the cat down the steep stairs. He carried it back to his small cold bedroom. He put it on the bed, and the cat curled into a small grey circle on his pillow as if it had always belonged there.

The boy lay down beside it. The house was quiet now. The wind sang softly against the windows.

He smiled in the dark.

In the morning, he would tell his mother that the old house had given them a gift. And he would never, again in his life, be quite so afraid of the dark.

stories.title: The Other Door
stories.text:
# The Other Door

The door appeared in the studio wall on the longest night of the year, and the woman knew, with a strange and tired calm, that she had been waiting for it.

She was forty-six years old. She had not painted anything in eleven months. The studio above the flower shop was small and cold, and the heater was making the soft clicking sound it always made when she had forgotten, again, to fill it with oil. Outside, snow was falling on the narrow street. Inside, three blank canvases leaned against the wall, accusing her, the way they had been accusing her for almost a year.

She had been about to go downstairs and lock up for the night when she saw it.

The door was set into the back wall of the studio, between the old cupboard and the radiator. The wall, until ten seconds ago, had been a wall. The door was wooden, painted a soft, faded green, with a small brass handle. It looked as though it had been there for fifty years. It looked, in fact, exactly like the door of her grandmother's house in the village she had not visited since she was nineteen.

She did not scream. She did not even gasp. She simply put down the cup of cold tea she had been holding, and she walked slowly toward the door, and she stood in front of it for a long time.

Then she opened it.

Beyond the door was a room she had never been in, and yet she recognized it instantly.

It was a wide, sunlit kitchen. The light was the warm yellow of late afternoon — not winter light, summer light. There was a long wooden table, and on the table were paint tubes, brushes, jars of cloudy water, and three half-finished canvases. The canvases were beautiful. Strange and confident and alive in a way her own work had not been since she was thirty. A radio was playing softly in another room. Somewhere, a dog was scratching at a door.

A woman walked into the kitchen.

The woman was the same age as her. The woman was, in fact, her — but lighter, somehow. Her hair was longer. Her hands had paint on them. Her face had the small, settled lines of a person who had been doing what she loved for a long time, without much money, and with no regret.

The other woman saw her at the door and stopped. She did not look frightened. She looked, instead, as if she had been half expecting this for years.

"You came," the other woman said.

"I do not know how I am here."

"No one ever does. Come in. The kettle is on."

The woman stepped through the door. Behind her, the cold studio was still visible — the blank canvases, the clicking heater, the snow falling past the window. Ahead of her was warm yellow afternoon light and the smell of turpentine and something baking.

She sat at the long wooden table. The other version of herself poured tea.

"You stayed," the woman said quietly. It was not a question.

"I stayed." The other woman sat down across from her. "I did not take the office job. I did not move to the city. I did not marry the man who told me painting was a hobby." She said it without bitterness. She said it the way you describe roads on a map.

"And you have been happy?"

The other woman thought about this. She turned her cup slowly in her hands — the same gesture, the woman noticed, that she herself made when she was thinking.

"Not always," she said finally. "There were years when I had no money. There was a winter when the heat was cut off and I painted in a coat. There was a man I loved who left because I was always working. I did not avoid pain. I avoided a different pain. That is all any of us do."

The woman was silent. The radio in the other room played a song she half-remembered from when she was young.

"Why did the door come?" she asked.

The other woman smiled, gently, the way you smile at someone you used to be.

"It comes when you are tired enough to look at it," she said. "It does not come to make you regret. It comes to ask you a question."

"What question?"

"Whether you are still alive."

The woman looked down at her own hands. They were the hands of a person who had, for many years, made sensible choices. They had taken her many places. They had built a small, careful life. They had not held a brush in eleven months.

She looked up. "Can I stay?"

The other woman shook her head, kindly. "This is not your kitchen. This was never your kitchen. You cannot have my life. That is not what the door is for."

"Then what is it for?"

"It is for you to remember," the other woman said softly, "that you also made a choice. And that you are still allowed to make another one."

The woman sat for a long time in the warm sunlit kitchen of a life she had not lived. The other version of herself did not rush her. The tea cooled. The dog in the other room stopped scratching. Somewhere, very faintly, she could hear the clicking of a small heater that needed oil.

Finally, she stood.

"Thank you," she said.

"Go," the other woman said gently. "And paint something tonight. Anything. It does not have to be good. It only has to be yours."

The woman walked back through the door. She heard it close softly behind her. She did not turn around to look. She suspected, correctly, that the wall was a wall again.

The studio was cold. The snow was still falling. The three blank canvases were still leaning against the wall.

She took off her coat. She filled the heater with oil. She pulled the smallest canvas onto the easel. She squeezed a little blue paint onto a plate.

It was not good. The brush felt strange in her hand, like a tool she had borrowed and forgotten how to return.

But it was hers. And it was the longest night of the year, and somewhere ahead of her, a morning was coming.

She painted until the sky began to turn grey. Then she made herself a fresh cup of tea, and she sat down on the cold floor of her studio, and for the first time in eleven months, she felt something quiet and serious and almost forgotten.

She felt awake.

stories.title: The Quiet Boy
stories.text:
# The Quiet Boy

The other children had been walking for ten minutes before the girl noticed that the quiet boy was not with them.

It was an autumn morning. The sky was pale and clear. The whole class was walking from the small village school to the lake, the way they did every year. The teacher walked at the front. The children walked in noisy pairs behind her. Their shoes made a happy sound on the dirt road. Yellow leaves were falling all around them.

The girl walked alone, near the back. She was new this year, like the quiet boy, but she had made one friend already and she was not afraid. The quiet boy had not made any friends. He had been at the school for three weeks, and in three weeks, he had not said one word.

"He is strange," the other children said.

"He thinks he is too good for us," they said.

"My mother says his family is not normal," they said.

The girl had never said any of these things. She had only watched him. He sat at the back of the classroom. He drew small pictures in the corner of his notebook when he thought no one was looking. The pictures were beautiful — birds, mostly, and small careful trees. Once, when he had dropped his pencil and she had picked it up, his eyes had met hers, and she had seen something there that was not strange or proud. Something more like a boy who was very, very tired.

Now she stopped on the dirt road and looked back.

The quiet boy was sitting on a low stone wall about two hundred metres behind. He was holding his ankle. Even from here, she could see that his face was white.

She looked at the front of the line. The teacher was talking to the bigger children about the names of trees. No one had noticed.

The girl turned around and walked back.

"Are you alright?" she said, when she reached him.

The quiet boy looked up at her, surprised. He did not answer.

"Your foot," she said.

He pointed at a hole in the ground beside the stone wall. He had stepped in it. His ankle was already turning purple.

The girl knelt down. She had three older brothers. She knew about hurt ankles. "Can you stand up?"

The quiet boy tried. He stood. He took one step. He sat back down on the wall and closed his eyes.

"Wait here," she said. "I will run and get the teacher."

The quiet boy shook his head, hard. He looked frightened.

"Why?" she said.

He pointed up the road, where the rest of the class was walking away. He pointed at himself. He shook his head again.

She understood. He did not want them to see him like this. He did not want to be the one who slowed everyone down. He did not want to give the other children one more thing to laugh at.

The girl sat down on the wall beside him.

"Then we will not call them," she said.

He looked at her, surprised again.

"My grandmother lives near here," she said. "In the white house with the blue gate. We can walk slowly. She will give us tea, and she will call your mother. The class will not see."

The quiet boy looked at her for a long moment. Then, very slowly, he nodded.

She helped him stand. He put one arm across her shoulders. He was lighter than she expected. They walked together, very slowly, down a small side path between the trees. He did not say anything. She did not need him to.

It took them almost an hour to reach her grandmother's house. The girl talked the whole way — about her grandmother's three cats, about the funny old radio in her kitchen, about the time her brother had fallen out of the apple tree. The quiet boy did not answer. But once, when she said something about the apple tree, she heard a small soft sound beside her. A laugh. The smallest laugh in the world. She did not look at him. She did not want him to feel watched. But she smiled at the road ahead of her, and she kept talking.

At her grandmother's house, the old woman opened the door, took one look at the boy's ankle, and went straight to the kitchen for warm water and a clean cloth. She called his mother. She made tea. She gave them both a piece of the cake she had baked that morning.

The quiet boy ate the cake slowly, as if he had forgotten how to be inside a warm kitchen with people who were not angry.

When his mother came to take him home, he stopped in the doorway. He turned around. He looked at the girl.

"Thank you," he said.

It was the first time anyone at the school had heard his voice.

The next morning at school, his ankle was bandaged, and he sat at the back of the classroom as always. The other children whispered about him. The girl walked across the room, in front of everyone, and she sat down in the empty seat beside him.

He did not speak. He did not need to.

He slid his notebook a little toward her, so she could see the small careful drawing of a bird he was making in the corner.

She smiled and took out her own pencil.

stories.title: The First Morning
stories.text:
# The First Morning

The boat was still tied to the small wooden dock, and the boy was the only one there to untie it.

The lake was very quiet. The sun had not come up yet. The water was grey and smooth, like the inside of a shell. A thin white mist sat on top of it, soft and slow. Somewhere in the trees, a bird was making its first small sound of the morning. The boy stood on the dock with his fishing rod in one hand and a small bucket in the other, and he looked at the boat, and the boat looked back at him.

He was eleven years old. He had been coming to this lake with his grandfather every summer since he was four.

Every morning, before the sun came up, his grandfather would wake him gently. They would walk down the path together, the old man and the boy, and they would untie the small wooden boat, and they would row out to the middle of the lake to fish. His grandfather had taught him everything. How to hold the rod. How to read the water. How to wait.

"You are not ready yet to go alone," his grandfather always said, smiling. "Maybe next year."

This morning, his grandfather had not woken up to come.

The boy had walked down the wooden hallway of his grandparents' small house at four o'clock. The door of his grandfather's bedroom had been closed. His grandmother had been sitting in the kitchen, in her old grey robe, with a cup of tea that she was not drinking.

"He is not well today," she had said softly. "His chest. The doctor is coming this afternoon."

"Is it bad?" the boy had asked.

"It is not good," his grandmother had said. She had tried to smile. "He told me to tell you. He said you can go to the dock if you like, just to look at the water. He said the lake is good for the heart in the morning."

That had been twenty minutes ago.

Now the boy stood on the dock, and his hands were holding things they had only ever held when his grandfather was beside him.

He could go back to the house. That was what a younger boy would do. His grandfather had not said *take the boat out*. His grandfather had said *go and look at the water*.

But the boy was thinking about something else.

He was thinking about how his grandfather's hands had shaken yesterday, when the old man had tried to open a jar at dinner. He was thinking about how thin his grandfather's shoulders had become this summer. He was thinking, with a small cold feeling in his stomach, that maybe there were not many more mornings on this dock. Maybe there were not many more *next years*.

And if his grandfather got better — when his grandfather got better, he made himself say — the boy wanted to come home with a fish. A real fish, that he had caught himself, alone. He wanted to put it on the kitchen table and say *I went out alone, and I caught this for you.* He wanted to see his grandfather's face when he said it.

He was afraid.

He untied the boat anyway.

The rope was rougher in his hands than he remembered. The boat felt smaller without his grandfather sitting in the back of it. He climbed in carefully. He sat down. He took the oars. They were too long for his arms, the way they had always been too long for his arms, but his grandfather had shown him a way to hold them that worked.

He began to row.

The boat moved slowly out into the grey lake. The mist parted around him in small white circles. He rowed until he reached the place his grandfather always took him — the deep water, near the old fallen tree, where the big fish came up at dawn. He pulled the oars in. He let the boat drift.

He baited his hook with hands that were almost steady.

He cast the line.

For a long time, nothing happened. The sun began to rise behind the mountains. The mist on the water turned pink, then gold. A second bird started singing in the trees. The boy sat very still in the small boat, alone, in the middle of the quiet lake, and he did not feel small anymore. He felt something else. Something he did not have a word for yet, but which felt a little like the way his grandfather's hand had felt on his shoulder, all the summers of his life.

The line jumped.

The boy lifted the rod the way he had been taught — slow, then firm. He did not panic. He did not pull too hard. He held the line with both hands and he listened to the fish the way his grandfather had taught him to listen, and after a few long minutes, he brought it up out of the dark water.

It was not the biggest fish he had ever seen. It was not the smallest, either. It was a real fish, silver and surprised, flashing in the early light.

The boy held it carefully. His hands were shaking now, but in a different way.

He rowed back to the dock. He tied the boat the way his grandfather had shown him. He carried the fish up the path in the small bucket, and the morning birds were loud now, and the sun was warm on his face.

In the kitchen, his grandmother stood up when she saw him. She put both hands over her mouth.

"Is he awake?" the boy asked quietly.

"He is awake," she said. "Go."

The boy walked down the wooden hallway with the bucket in his hands. He pushed open the door of his grandfather's room. The old man was sitting up against his pillows, his face thin and tired, but smiling — already smiling, before he had even seen the bucket, as if he had known.

"I went out alone," the boy said.

His grandfather's eyes were wet. He nodded slowly.

"I know you did," he said. "I heard the boat."

stories.title: The Wrong Town
stories.text:
# The Wrong Town

The woman had been off the train for exactly four minutes when she realized that this was not, in any meaningful sense, the town she had booked.

She was standing on a small platform that did not have her town's name on it. The sign on the wall said something else entirely — a shorter name, with one of those soft regional letters she had not learned to pronounce. The platform had two benches, one ticket machine, a single sleeping cat on a window ledge, and a printed schedule from, she suspected, several years ago. She turned a slow, professional circle. There was no other train. There was no station master. There was, at the far end of the platform, a small handwritten sign that said, in a friendly cursive she did not trust: *Welcome, dear traveller!*

She took a long breath. She closed her eyes. She opened them.

The sign still said *Welcome, dear traveller!*

She checked her phone. Her itinerary, which she had printed out *and* saved as a PDF *and* memorized, said: *Day Two — arrive 14:42, hotel check-in by 15:30, walking tour of historical centre at 16:00.* It was 15:08. The historical centre, according to a local map she had now anxiously zoomed in on, was approximately forty-one kilometres south of where she was standing.

She pulled her small, neat suitcase down the platform with the dignified speed of a woman pretending nothing was wrong.

At the only café in the town — there really was only one — a man behind the counter was reading a newspaper. He looked up when she came in. He smiled the smile of a person whose café did not get a lot of urgent foreign tourists.

"I was supposed to get off at the next stop," she said carefully.

"Ah," he said. "Yes. Many people do this. The names are similar." He shrugged, as if this explained something deeply philosophical about the universe.

"When is the next train back?"

"Tomorrow morning."

"There is no train this evening?"

"There is a train," he said kindly. "It does not stop here."

She stared at him. He stared back, friendly, unhelpful, completely at peace. Outside, the sleeping cat had not moved.

The woman tried, on her phone, to book a taxi for forty-one kilometres south. There were no taxis. She tried a car rental. The nearest one was, she was informed cheerfully by an automated reply, in the town she had been *trying* to reach. She tried the hotel she had booked, to explain. The hotel said, also cheerfully, that they would charge her the night anyway because she had not cancelled before noon.

She sat down at one of the café's three small tables.

"You are upset," the café man observed gently.

"I am organized," she said. "Those are different things."

He nodded. He poured her a coffee she had not ordered, and put a small plate of something pastry-shaped beside it. "On the house," he said. "For the dear traveller."

She wanted, very badly, to say something cool and ironic. Instead, she ate the pastry. It was excellent. It was, in fact, the best pastry she had eaten in years — flaky and warm and faintly sweet with something she could not identify and did not want to ask about, in case asking spoiled it. She had a second one. She had not had a second pastry since she was nineteen.

The café man, who had introduced himself by now as the owner, the cook, the waiter, and "sometimes also the tourist office," recommended a small family-run guesthouse three streets away. He recommended a walk to the old harbour at sunset. He recommended a particular fish dish at a particular small restaurant which, he warned her seriously, did not have a sign and was located behind a different restaurant.

She wrote none of this down, which was, for her, a radical act.

The guesthouse was run by a woman named — well, the name took her three tries to say, which both of them found funny. The room had one window. The window faced the harbour. The harbour, when she finally walked down to it that evening, was not in any guidebook she had ever read, and she suspected this was because the guidebook writers had also, probably, gotten off at the right station like the well-organized people they were, and missed it entirely.

The sunset was absurd. It was the kind of sunset that, if you painted it, people would politely tell you that you had overdone the colours.

She found the restaurant behind the other restaurant. She ate the fish. The fish was, of course, the best fish she had ever eaten.

Walking back to the guesthouse in the warm spring dark, she passed a small square where four old men were playing a card game she did not understand, with great seriousness, while a fifth old man watched and gave occasional advice that was, judging from the reactions, deeply insulting. One of them looked up, saw her, and lifted a hand in greeting, as though she had been walking past this square every evening for thirty years.

She lifted her hand back.

In her room, she sat on the bed and looked at her itinerary. *Day Three — historical walking tour, part two. Day Four — boat trip. Day Five — wine region.* She read it the way you read a letter from a person you used to know. She liked that woman. She wished her well. She did not entirely want to be her this week.

She took out a pen and, with some effort, drew a single neat line through the rest of the schedule.

Then she added, in her careful handwriting: *Day Three — ask the café man what is good. Try the second pastry first.*

She turned out the light. Outside, the harbour was quiet. Somewhere, a boat made a small wooden sound against the dock.

She slept, and she slept long, and in the morning, for the first time in a long time, she did not check the clock before she opened her eyes.

stories.title: The Tuesday Flowers
stories.text:
# The Tuesday Flowers

Every Tuesday morning, the yellow flowers were there.

The young girl had noticed them three weeks ago. She lived next door to the old woman, in a small house on a quiet street. The old woman lived alone. Her husband had died many years ago. Her children lived in another city. She did not get many visitors.

But every Tuesday, when the girl walked to school at half past seven, there was a small fresh bunch of yellow flowers sitting on the old woman's doorstep. Just sitting there. No card. No paper. No name.

The girl had asked her mother about it.

"Maybe a friend," her mother had said.

The girl had asked the old woman about it, gently.

"I do not know who brings them," the old woman had said, smiling. "But I am very happy. I put them in water. They make the kitchen bright."

The girl decided she would find out.

The next Tuesday, she got up very early. The sky was still grey. The street was empty. She sat by her bedroom window with her mother's old binoculars and she watched the old woman's doorstep.

At six o'clock, nothing happened.

At six fifteen, a black cat walked past. Then nothing again.

At six thirty, the milk man came. He left two bottles. He did not leave flowers.

At six forty-five, the girl was beginning to fall asleep against the window.

At six fifty-three, she saw him.

A small boy. Maybe seven years old. He was carrying a bunch of yellow flowers in both hands. He walked up the street very slowly, looking around, the way you look around when you are doing something secret. He stopped at the old woman's gate. He opened it carefully. He put the flowers on the doorstep. Then he ran away, fast, down the street.

The girl knew that boy. He lived three houses away.

She got dressed and she went outside.

She walked to his house. His mother was in the garden, hanging up clothes.

"Excuse me," the girl said. "Why does your son leave flowers for the old woman every Tuesday?"

The mother stopped. She put down the wet shirt in her hands. She looked at the girl for a long moment. Then she sat down slowly on the small garden step.

"He has not told me he was doing this," she said softly. "But I think I know why."

The girl waited.

"Last winter," the mother said, "my son was walking home from school. It was very cold. He had forgotten his gloves. He was crying because his hands hurt. The old woman saw him from her window. She came out. She gave him a pair of warm woollen gloves. Yellow ones. She told him they had belonged to her son when he was small. She said he should keep them."

The mother was smiling now, but her eyes were wet.

"My son has worn those gloves every day this winter," she said. "And in the spring, when the yellow flowers came up in our garden, I think he wanted to say thank you. But he is shy. He does not know how to say it with words."

The girl walked home slowly.

That afternoon, after school, she knocked on the old woman's door. She told her the story — gently, carefully, the way she would want someone to tell her.

The old woman listened. She did not speak for a long time. Then she went into her kitchen. She came back with a small wooden box. Inside the box was a pair of small yellow woollen gloves, very old, very soft.

"My son was seven when he wore these," the old woman said. "He died when he was nine. I have kept these gloves for forty years."

She closed the box gently.

"I gave them to a small cold boy in the winter," she said, "because forty years is a long time to keep something just for yourself."

The next Tuesday, when the yellow flowers appeared on the old woman's doorstep, there was a small note beside them this time. The note was written in a child's handwriting.

It said: *Thank you for the gloves.*

And next to the note, the old woman placed her own small note, in her careful old writing, for the boy to find when he came back the following week.

It said: *Thank you for the flowers.*
